To fix (3)

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 3 imprecise p values out of 22 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p < 0.05 All 19 novel loci showed a consistent direction of effect, with p < 0.05, in the cohorts other than FinnGen (Table S4).
p < 0.05 In contrast, local genetic correlation with BMI was close to zero in 15 of the 16 testable blocks with nominal (p < 0.05) local correlation with HS.
p > 0.6 The set showed the same direction in META_EUR (p = 7×10 -5 ), and it was not associated with HS, acne or BMI (p > 0.6).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = 0.89 In a model of PSD on HS and BMI, HS was associated with PSD (standardised β = 0.75, SE 0.13, p = 1×10 -8 ), whereas BMI was not (β = 0.01, p = 0.89).
p > 0.6 The set showed the same direction in META_EUR (p = 7×10 -5 ), and it was not associated with HS, acne or BMI (p > 0.6).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

We recommend the .zip format for archives: only ZIP stores its file listing in a way that lets a tool inspect the contents without downloading the whole archive, so a .zip is more discoverable and re-usable than a .7z, .rar, .tar or .tar.gz.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 1 code file.

File name setwd() calls found
04d_genomic_sem.R setwd(file.path(base, “results”))

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 986 columns across 64 data files.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 64 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • 04b_coloc_psd_vs_traits.R reads HS.tsv.gz.
  • 01c_finemap_psd_loci.py reads plink2.
  • 05a_eqtl_coloc_gtex.R reads ensembl105_genes.tsv.
  • 09a_lead_variant_supplementary_table.py reads psd_leads_grch37.json.
  • 10a_format_gwas_catalog.py reads indel_rsids_grch38.json.
  • 11b_paper_miami.py reads miami_thinned.tsv.gz.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A package could not be installed.

  • 04c_lava_local_rg.R needs LAVA.
  • 04d_genomic_sem.R needs GenomicSEM.

LAVA is not on CRAN, and your code does not say where it comes from. If it comes from GitHub or Bioconductor, install it at the top of the script, or name the command in the README, for example remotes::install_github(“user/LAVA”) or BiocManager::install(“LAVA”), with the version you used.

GenomicSEM is not on CRAN, and your code does not say where it comes from. If it comes from GitHub or Bioconductor, install it at the top of the script, or name the command in the README, for example remotes::install_github(“user/GenomicSEM”) or BiocManager::install(“GenomicSEM”), with the version you used.

R or Python could not read a script, because of a mistake in the code itself.

  • 04a_prepare_shared_genetics_inputs.py

Run each script once in a fresh session before you deposit it; the error message shows the line to fix.

A script downloads data while it runs.

  • 07a_locus_to_gene_table.py

Online files can move, change or disappear. Save the downloaded files, add them to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copies.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

Other problems in the files

  • 04d_genomic_sem.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 5 statistical tests reported in the paper, 0 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 5 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 04b_coloc_psd_vs_traits.R — numeric
2 04c_lava_local_rg.R — numeric
3 04d_genomic_sem.R — numeric
4 05a_eqtl_coloc_gtex.R — numeric
5 psd_genetics_talk.qmd — none

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 2 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: blocks_s2500_m25_f1_w200.grch37_hg19.locfile, ensembl105_genes.tsv.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 5 scripts: 1 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 2 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

Dependency-unavailable errors

2 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so it does not force the traffic light red.

File
04c_lava_local_rg.R
04d_genomic_sem.R

setwd() in the code

1 script calls setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set
